title: Extra fingers and too much detail: Rise in AI-generated tattoo requests
text:
Tattoo artists are concerned about customers increasingly requesting designs based on AI-generated images, which they say often contain errors and set "unrealistic expectations".

Adelaide tattoo artist Courtnii Shaw said about one in four enquiries her studio received included AI imagery.

She said sometimes the enquiries themselves appeared AI-generated.

"We're getting entirely [AI-]generated enquiries of people telling ChatGPT what they want and then they're copying that to us," she said.

"It's really, really common now. People seem to really trust what AI gives them and tells them, so I find that it's just setting some unrealistic expectations."

AI-generated tattoo designs can have too much detail or contain errors, such as adding an extra finger. (Supplied by Phil Pagdin)

At Phil Pagdin's studio, the number of enquiries containing AI-generated tattoos was closer to three in four.

He said the imagery tended to look repetitive, highly detailed and often contained errors — which some clients were not aware about.

"There's some obvious ones where it'll spell something wrong," he said.

"When we talk to the client about their design, we're like, 'Oh, what is this part here?' and they don't even know.

" You're going to come up with a weird tattoo that you can't really read. "

Phil Pagdin says some of the AI tattoo designs contained spelling mistakes. (Supplied: Phil Pagdin)

Brenton Eldridge, vice president of the Professional Tattooing Association of Australia, said AI-generated imagery was "pressuring" young artists to perform.

"A person will come to the studio, present that [AI image] and want a quote on it … they're not really in a good mindset to be told it's not practical, or it's going to take a hundred hours when AI is generated in one minute," he said.

"It's creating a bit of conflict."

Tattoo artists have observed a rise in AI-generated tattoo images appearing in customer requests. (Supplied: Phil Pagdin)

AI a good tool with limitations

But Mr Eldridge said AI could be useful for artists in the development phase of a design.

"AI itself can be a fantastic tool for artists to use to prototype things, look at different effects, and quickly throw something together," he said.

"But in the way of a tattoo client, it's very difficult because clients are not aware of what can be done in the skin, how the designs will heal over time and grow and colour change.

"AI cannot take that into account."

Paul Briske says AI does not take into account where designs are placed on the body. (Supplied: Paul Briske)

Tattoo artist and studio owner Paul Briske said careful consideration was given to where designs could be placed on the body — something AI could not take into account.

"Tattoos have to be done at a certain size for the details to hold over time," he said.

"There are tiny, intricate little details that people want to see on a hand or a leg, and they just cannot physically be done to that level."

Mr Briske encouraged people to embrace their creativity, and not rely too heavily on AI.

"The biggest shame out of all of this computer stuff, it was supposed to take away all the menial jobs so that we had time to enjoy art and express ourselves," he said.

"Unfortunately, it's done the opposite and it's doing the art for us."

Courtnii Shaw says the best part of a tattoo artist's job is creating the design. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

The artists urged people wanting to get a tattoo to slow down and embrace the collaborative process.

"We understand that being able to visualise your tattoo idea on your own and having it immediately available feels like a really cool thing," Ms Shaw said.

"But it is also the best part of our job, which is creating the design."

title: Birthday boy Popyrin wins in Montreal
text:
Alexei Popyrin has celebrated turning 27 by booking his place in the Montreal Masters' round of 32 for the third year running.

The shock 2024 champion progressed in just 76 minutes, beating the 32nd-seeded Belgian Raphaël Collignon 6-4, 6-3 on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Former world number 19 but currently ranked 139, Popyrin beat fellow Australian Thanasi Kokkinakis to earn his place in the main draw and saw off Román Andrés Burruchaga in round one to notch his first ATP-level win since May.

And with another crack looming at the US Open in New York — where he beat Novak Djokovic in 2024 en route to his best finish at Flushing Meadows — Popyrin can largely credit another win in Canada to his booming serve.

Popyirn fired down 10 aces, won 84 per cent (27/32) of first-serve points and did not face a break point, while also converting three of nine break-point opportunities of his own.

The Sydneysider will next face another Argentine in Thiago Tirante, who upset world number 9 and seventh-seeded American Taylor Fritz 7-5, 6-3.

At the women's WTA event in Toronto meantime, Australian world number 61 Daria Kasatkina suffered a lengthy, 6-3, 5-7, 6-4 loss to second seed Elena Rybakina.

The two-time grand slam champion from Kazakhstan survived after a two-hour and 22-minute scare to progress and tee up a clash with 28th seed Anna Li of the US.

Later on Wednesday, 20-year-old Aussie qualifier Maya Joint beat 14th-seeded Romanian Sorana Cîrstea 6-4, 6-4 to join compatriot Talia Gibson in the third round.

AAP

title: AFLPA responds after report says player signed concussion deal with club
text:
The AFL Players Association says it is in discussions with the league after reports a Victorian club signed a deal with a player with a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

According to a report in News Corp newspapers on Thursday, the club made the player sign the agreement in a bid to exonerate itself and its medical staff from future court action.

The deal with the unnamed footballer, who is still an active AFL player, was signed two years ago.

The report said the club viewed such an agreement as the only way the player could continue his career given his history of concussions.

Loading...

The disclosure agreement required the individual to "take upon yourself the physical and legal risk of loss, damage or injury" arising from future concussions.

It also acknowledged the player was at higher risk of more concussions and could face more serious damage if they suffered further head knocks.

The reported deal has been slammed by concussion campaigners, experts and the AFL Players Association (AFLPA), who were reportedly unaware of the agreement.

"Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and Standard Playing Contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws," AFLPA boss James Gallagher said in a statement provided to ABC Sport.

'I have lost basically everything': Ex-AFL player opens up on compensation fight Head trauma ended Aiden O'Driscoll's promising AFL career before he could play his first game. Now, like many former footballers affected by brain injuries, he faces an uncertain future as he fights for compensation.

"Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so.

"We are in discussions with AFL to better understand the circumstances of this case and ensure this issue is not replicated further at the elite level."

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL today.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley and Shane Tuck, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

title: ACT opposition leader admits to texting 'f*** my job is boring' during hearing
text:
ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton has admitted he sent a text message complaining about how boring his job is during budget estimates.

In a press conference on Thursday morning, the Canberra Liberals leader admitted to sending a text that said "f*** my job is boring" but did not reveal who he sent it to.

A complaint was previously lodged against him alleging Mr Parton had sent the text to a sex worker, something he denies.

A screenshot of Mark Parton's lemon8 social media account. (Supplied)

But today, Mr Parton said he had been told the standards commissioner would not be investigating the allegations made in the complaint.

"I was contacted by the standards commissioner last night, who wrote to me to advise that he had received an anonymous complaint, but he had made the call not to investigate further, and he was obliged to do that," Mr Parton said.

When approached by the ABC, Commissioner Ken Crispin said he could not comment on individual complaints.

However, he confirmed he would not investigate a complaint if there was insufficient evidence, if the complaint was frivolous in nature or if there was political motivation behind the complaint.

Asked if he had sent the text to a sex worker, Mr Parton said: "The complaint has been dismissed".

"It's not being investigated by the standards commissioner, and as such I just don't regard it to be in the public interest," he said.

Asked again if he denied he was texting with a sex worker, Mr Parton said: "Yeah, I do".

Mr Parton was also asked if he had ever "engaged" with sex workers.

"Again, I'm sorry. There was an anonymous complaint that's been made that has been dismissed by the standards commissioner," he replied.

"I'm not going to entertain questions that are completely removed from that and that are not in the public interest. I'm just not going there."

But asked by the ABC if he had texted "f*** my job is boring", Mr Parton said: "Yes I did".

He defended the content of the text message, saying he was still "holding the government to account".

"There's a hell of a lot of private messages that are sent from a hell of a lot of people in the context of sitting days and hearings," he said.

" To be honest, I'm not sure that they're really anybody's business other than the sender and the receiver. "

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton says he does not know who made the complaint about him. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

'Multi-tasker from hell'

The text message was sent on Friday while Mr Parton was in a hearing discussing plans to redevelop Telstra Tower in consultation with the local Ngunnawal community.

Mr Parton, who is the Canberra Liberals spokesman for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs, replied that he was "a multi-tasker from hell".

"I think it's appropriate to send private messages to people that are not designed for the public realm," he said.

" And I think those of you who've known me for long enough would know that I've got an off-the-cuff larrikin communication style. "

But he said, "most people's perception of budget estimates hearings is that they're pretty boring".

"Now, again, I'm of the belief that we're able to prosecute some pretty solid things in those hearings, and that's what we'll continue to do, but we're also humans," he said.

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton denies he sent a text message saying his job was boring to a sex worker. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

He said he had been working long hours, including an 80-hour week recently.

"I've even posted — made social media posts while I'm in a hearing because there's only so much time in the day. And so you just get through what you can get through," he said.

"I don't think anyone can question how much time and effort that I'm putting into this job.

"And I'm happy to be judged on the outcomes that I'm getting, the fact that I am genuinely holding this government to account in an extremely robust way and that I am doing the best that I can do every single day."

'Clear attempt to smear'

In a statement sent by a spokesperson last night, Mr Parton said the allegations were "a clear attempt to smear".

"Mr Parton first became aware of the complaint Monday morning. He rejects the allegations in full," the statement said.

The spokesperson also said Mr Parton had referred the matter to the Australian Federal Police.

Asked today why he had taken that step, he said he was being "damaged" by "bad actors".

"Because on occasions when there are some actors who are trying to cause damage to you, I think it's warranted to make the call to have some matters investigated and that's what we'll be seeking to do again with this," he said.

Mark Parton took on leadership of the Canberra Liberals in November 2025. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

Estimates 'an important part of our political process': Barr

Speaking to the ABC, Chief Minister Andrew Barr said he had a brief text exchange with Mr Parton on Thursday morning, but said the matter did not involve him or the government.

"I take on face value the opposition leader's very strong denial of the allegations," he said.

" I am certainly not seeking to score any political points here, it is ultimately not really my business. "

He described budget estimates as a "long process", adding he would not be "surprised" if someone was bored during a budget estimates hearing.

"Whether you need to text that to someone is another matter," he said.

"It's a busy two weeks, but it is an important part of our political process."

title: Inquest into mother's death examines Albury Hospital transfer delays
text:
Kate Manley's family remember her as a strong, independent mother who was full of energy and brought laughter into the lives of everyone who knew her before she died at Albury Wodonga Health's Albury hospital.

Ms Manley died on November 16, 2022 of a suspected pulmonary embolism, a blood clot emergency closely related to deep vein thrombosis.

A five-day inquest into her death has concluded at Albury Local Court.

On Tuesday, counsel assisting the coroner Patrick Rooney read a family statement issued by her twin brother Alex to the court.

"[Kate] was compassionate, creative and had drive … [and] brought fun, warmth and laughter into the lives of those who knew her," the family statement said.

The 46-year-old qualified chef was described as being the glue that held the family together, with her daughter Ruby "the centre of her world".

Kate Manley was remembered by family as someone who was "independent, strong, beautiful and full of energy". (Supplied: Manley family)

Evidence from several Albury Wodonga Health (AWH) staff, executives and medical experts was provided to the inquest.

Ms Manley was diagnosed with catatonia not long after presenting at the hospital on November 11, after medical staff said she had minimal responses when they attempted to speak to her.

She died in the hospital's medical ward five days later, having been admitted to Nolan House, the mental acute psychiatric ward located at Albury Hospital.

Five-hour wait for patient transfer

The court heard Ms Manley had waited five hours to be transferred from Nolan House to the medical ward, where her blood-clot risk could be assessed.

"Obviously and tragically, further examination and treatment would have occurred at the medical ward if there had been more time," Mr Rooney told Coroner Rebecca Hosking.

The inquest has heard communication issues between wards at the hospital may have led to Kate Manley's death. (Supplied: Albury Wodonga Health)

Mr Rooney said there were communication issues between Nolan House and medical ward staff as to the severity of Ms Manley's deteriorating condition.

Issues over patient tracking systems

The inquest also examined how the location of Nolan House may have impacted the events leading up to Ms Manley's death.

The unit is located at Albury in NSW, but is administered under Victorian laws.

Kate Manley, 46, died of a pulmonary embolism at Albury Hospital on November 16, 2022. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

During hearings on Tuesday, acting director of mental health and wellbeing Dannielle McLeish said the hospital had several combined systems in place to track patient movements.

She told the court that the inclusion of paper-based systems, which were required under Victorian laws, in addition to electronic tracking systems, was challenging to manage and confusing for staff.

"It's important to have a single source for the location of a patient," Ms McLeish said.

Former AWH interim CEO Andrew Way had given a statement prior to the inquest saying that from information provided to him, communication between Nolan House and the medical ward was "ineffective".

On Tuesday, Professor Way told the court that during his short three-month tenure as interim CEO, he made efforts to go to Nolan House to talk with frontline staff to discuss those issues.

"Whilst I would admit that they're not perfect, they struck me as being consistent with what I would have expected of a unit of this scale and size," he told the court.

Steps already taken to improve transfers

In his submission, Mr Rooney referred to a previous coronial inquest into the death of Roger Schnelle at Nolan House.

A recommendation from that coronial investigation called for both NSW Health and Victoria's Department of Health to implement a sole electronic medical record across Albury Wodonga Health medical and mental health services.

He said AWH also encouraged that recommendation and such a record should be compatible with both NSW and Victorian systems.

Counsel acting for AWH, Lorna McFee, said the health service had already taken steps to improve patient transfers and other systems since Ms Manley's death.

She also submitted a statement from AWH's board members sharing their condolences to Ms Manley's family.

Coroner Hosking said that she expected to hand down findings and recommendations within a month.

title: Pineapple growers raise biosecurity concerns as Asian imports considered
text:
Australian pineapple growers fear a proposal to allow imports of the fruit from India and Indonesia could expose them to foreign pests and diseases.

The federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) has released a draft assessment report on the risks of importing decrowned pineapples after both countries requested market access under existing trade obligations.

The report found the fruit could be safely imported if strict biosecurity requirements were met to manage eight identified pests, most of which are species of mealy bugs.

Australia's annual pineapple production rose 16 per cent in the 2024-2025 financial year. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

But farmers believe imports are an unnecessary risk, as local fruit is meeting domestic demand.

While the assessment does not automatically mean trade will occur, farmers want risk management procedures to be closely scrutinised.

'Minimal uptake'

Second-generation grower Colin Hawken is worried the trade could open his farm at Mungar, south-west of Maryborough, to new threats.

"There are certain pests and diseases in India and Indonesia that we don't have here," he said.

"If we do get those diseases here, we've got nothing to fight them with."

Colin Hawken believes the Australian industry can meet domestic demand without imported fruit. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

As a member of the World Trade Organization, the department said Australia has international obligations it must meet, including assessing import proposals and developing conditions that are scientifically backed and don't unnecessarily restrict trade.

Under those obligations, the department cannot assess the potential economic impact of additional market competition, but it can rate the risks of identified pests and diseases.

Decrowning pineapples helps to remove potential pests hiding in the leaves. (ABC News: Meg Bolton )

Australia currently allows fresh decrowned pineapples to be imported from the Philippines, Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Taiwan, while import conditions are being finalised for Malaysia.

Australia received approximately 18 tonnes of pineapple from Taiwan in 2025, and there were no imports from any other country in the past five years.

Chief executive of Queensland Fruit and Vegetable Growers Scott Kompo-Harms said the imports were not needed.

Scott Kompo-Harms, chief executive of Queensland Fruit and Vegetable Growers. (Supplied: QFVG)

"Australia's biosecurity is one of our greatest natural assets, and we need to protect that," he said.

" If there are control measures that are put in place, we want to see that they are being abided by over the long term with regular monitoring. "

To reduce the risk of pests, the DAFF report suggested treatments such as fumigation and irradiation and recommended unit inspections and traceability to the farm and packing houses.

Year-round supply

While Indonesia's and India's pineapple production surpasses Australia's, growers here believed there was enough supply to satisfy domestic demand.

In the 2024/25 financial year, Australian farms produced 68,373 tonnes of pineapples … more than two-thirds were sold as fresh fruit.

"We can provide pineapples 365 days a year, and we can look after our own market," Mr Hawken said.

"At the moment pineapples are a bit short, and we're receiving a premium price, but other times of the year we're certainly at or below cost of production."

The national farmgate value was estimated to be $78.6 million.

In recent years growers have invested in new varieties and marketing campaigns to make fresh pineapples more appealing as they competed with canned products.

Scott Maxwell says the draft risk analysis was a key topic at the industry's annual field day. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

Scott Maxwell, chairman of Australian Pineapples, said the momentum the industry has experienced could be at risk.

"Every imported pineapple that's bought is an Australian pineapple that's not bought from an Australian farmer, which affects Australian jobs," he said.

" Growers are very concerned because it affects their livelihoods, they're the ones left to clean up the mess if there is an incursion. "

Consultation open

The pineapple industry is making a formal submission in response to the draft report.

The consultation period runs until September 14.

Stakeholders' comments will inform the final report, which will include responses to technical issues.

That report is expected to be released in the second half of 2027, and even if importation is recommended, both India and Indonesia will need to demonstrate they can implement all required controls before trade can begin.

title: Netball's uniform debacle hints at bigger problem for women in sport
text:
The Diamonds' 2026 Commonwealth Games campaign may well go down in history for all the wrong reasons, remembered not only for a shock semi-final loss to Jamaica but also for the dress controversy that preceded it.

After the Diamonds' 99-38 demolition of Tonga, media coverage focused not on the lopsided result but on the ill-fitting dresses players tugged at throughout matches.

Players like Sophie Garbin may have insisted the outfits were fine, but as ABC journalist Britt Carter put it, "if a shooter has to pull it down more than 10 times in a quarter, how much of that energy could be re-directed?"

Loading Instagram content

For elite women athletes, the problem is not just the impact poor-fitting uniforms have on performance.

Research shows that many adolescent girls drop out of sport citing body image issues, while concerns about uniforms have also been identified as a barrier to participation.

These are not just problems for younger people or community sport.

The ABC and Deakin University's recent survey of elite Australian athletes in women's sport found that 25 per cent have negative feelings about their body image, while 44 per cent have experienced an eating disorder and/or disordered eating.

The latter figure is much higher than what the Butterfly Foundation, a national charity for anyone affected by eating disorders and body image issues, estimates at 17 per cent for the general population.

Teigan O'Shannassy wants to see women and girls feel more comfortable in their bodies on the netball court. (Getty: Sanka Vidanagama)

Sydney-based netballer Teigan O'Shannassy is one of those who lives with a history of eating disorders and disordered eating.

She argues more awareness about the struggles elite female athletes face is key.

Dresses an issue during Super Netball season

O'Shannassy, who the ABC interviewed before the Commonwealth Games, admitted having issues with the Swifts' dress in the most recent Super Netball season, with teammates seen adjusting them during some matches.

"When you're playing in a dress in front of thousands of people, you want to be able to perform, and don't want to have to think about how you look or how you feel in the dress," she told the ABC.

" If you're struggling with your body image, having to do that and put on something that you don't want to wear, or you don't feel comfortable in, is really hard. "

Teigan O'Shannassy (left) has played for the Canberra Giants and the Sydney Swifts in her netball career. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

O'Shannassy, 27, has previously been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa and remembers vividly the moment her career came to a crossroads.

If you or someone you know needs help: The Butterfly Foundation: National helpline 1800 ED HOPE (1800 33 4673)

She was playing for the Giants at the time, in the middle of COVID-19 lockdowns, and was about to leave with the team for a Queensland hub.

O'Shannassy was called into a meeting with her head coach, assistant coach, dietitian, doctor and physio and told she would be staying behind so she could see a dietitian and therapist weekly.

"Looking back, I think that was probably the best decision they could have made," she said.

"I think it was one of the best things that could have happened to me. But obviously I was absolutely gutted. I thought my career was over."

Those feelings intensified when the Giants told her they would not offer her another contract, but invited her to stay on as a training partner.

The Swifts called with the same offer before O'Shannassy decided to leave.

Netballer Teigan O'Shannassy has struggled with body image throughout her career in the national league. (Getty: James Worsfold)

"Something needed to change," she said.

"I just felt like I was stuck in this constant cycle of injuries and under-fuelling because I felt like I wasn't training [enough] and I didn't deserve to eat."

'The more we can talk about it, the better'

Given her personal experience, O'Shannassy says she was "unfortunately not surprised" by the results of the ABC and Deakin survey.

"When I was really struggling, I honestly thought I was the only person that was struggling with my body and food and having all these negative thoughts around it," she said.

"But since I've spoken up about it, people have come to me and said 'oh, I struggle with this too', which in a way I think is helpful, that we're so open about it.

"I think the more we can talk about it, the better. Even for me, talking about my body in a positive way is still something that I need to work on, and I think everyone can do that every day."

Teigan O'Shannassy now teaches other women about nutrition and health. (Getty: Brett Hemmings)

O'Shannassy, who has since trained as an associate nutritionist and runs a business called Tossed Together, is passionate about building community understanding of the unique challenges athletes face.

These include, in a team sport like netball, the pressure to be more like your teammates or competitors.

She remembers first coming through competitive pathways at 17 and having her body compared unfavourably to others by her coaches.

"We got told, 'you should be lifting this amount of weight, you should all look like this player, you should be able to do what certain players can do,'" she said.

"That stuck so much in my head. I'd have niggle after niggle and just felt like my body was never good enough.

"I just wanted to be like the other netballers who were so strong and looked like athletes."

By contrast, O'Shannassy described her younger self as "tall, lanky and uncoordinated", and says she "never felt like I looked like an athlete".

Teigan O'Shannassy began playing for the Canberra Giants in her late teens. (Getty: Mark Nolan)

The requirement to undertake body composition testing, including skin folds and DEXA scans, also bred unhealthy comparisons.

"I remember being 19, 20, and hearing some girls saying what body fat [percentage] they were, and thinking 'oh god, I'm a bit higher than them' and just freaking out about it," O'Shannassy said.

Social media exposes further body scrutiny

Danni Rowlands, the Butterfly Foundation's director of education initiatives, is a former state netballer herself and shares a similar story to O'Shannassy.

She was diagnosed with an eating disorder at age 21 and remembers skin fold testing significantly influencing how she felt about her body as a junior athlete.

A former netballer herself, Danni Rowlands now advocates for a shift in sporting cultures through the Butterfly Foundation. (Supplied.)

"I was identified as being too high in body composition, so I was supported through a dietitian to reduce body fat," she said.

"I went on to make the state team and play nationals, which was amazing, but unfortunately played the entire tournament with a stress fracture in my ankle, which was later identified as being caused by under-nourishment and over-training.

" That just kicked off this whole cycle at a very vulnerable age where I connected my weight to my worth and success as an athlete. "

Since retiring from sport, she has worked to shift sporting cultures, heading Butterfly Foundation's BodyKindSports initiative, which recognises adolescence as a vulnerable time for athletes' relationship with their body, particularly young girls.

"We want to protect and support athletes in those early pathways so that they can thrive, and that the consequence of participating in sport isn't a lifelong struggle with eating, training and poor body image," Rowlands said.

The Diamonds claimed the bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. (Getty: Lintao Zhang)

She holds particular concerns for contemporary women athletes who are more accessible to the public than ever on social media.

"This idea that athlete bodies are commodities and we can all have a piece of them, and critique as we want [online], absolutely adds a layer of pressure for athletes that makes it more intense than ever before," Rowlands said.

" There are intense appearance pressures on women athletes to look pretty, and feminine, but not too muscular, or too thin. They just can't win, which is tough. "

She added that when players do have issues with their uniforms, as in the Commonwealth Games example, this can generate further unwanted attention on their bodies.

"Looking at women across a lot of sports, there's much more exposure of body parts compared to men," she said.

"I think we have to ask: why is this the case? Is it because it's going to help them perform better, or is it because we're treating female bodies differently in sport?"

Uniforms a factor in girls dropping out of sport Studies show a large percentage of girls drop out of sport when they become teenagers. One of the contributing factors is the clothes they have to wear.

O'Shannassy admitted being under the spotlight, and being photographed or filmed constantly, added a layer of discomfort for those with body image issues.

"For a female, that can be really triggering. You're always being watched, and I think that's something that can be kind of daunting," she said.

"As an athlete, obviously it's such a cool job, and there's so many positive things that come out of it, but the highs are high, and the lows are low.

"If you've never done it, you just really don't know what it can be like."

Athletes 'not immune' to body image issues

Moving forward, both O'Shannassy and Rowlands shared messages of support for women in sport.

Rowlands encouraged athletes who might be struggling to "seek support sooner rather than later".

"Being an athlete doesn't make you immune to any of those pressures. If anything, it intensifies them further. So be kind to yourself, and if you are struggling, reach out," she said.

All Teigan O'Shannassy ever wanted to do in her life was play netball. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

O'Shannassy, meanwhile, hopes sharing her story will continue to inspire others who may be experiencing something similar.

Although her worst days are well behind her, she says it can help to acknowledge that an eating disorder is not "something you can just turn off, or wake up and you're fine".

"You might have that voice in your head forever," she said.

"For me, it's just, I hear that voice and I acknowledge it, but I don't let it control me anymore."

She says it is important to find the thing that motivates you to keep fighting, which for her has always been her chosen sport.

"For me it was netball, all I ever wanted to do was play netball," she said.

"And I knew that if I didn't eat or didn't fuel myself I was never going to get there."

title: FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan
text:
FIFA says it has apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to sell commercial rights linked to the World Cup, as the governing body's leadership reaffirmed its support for president Gianni Infantino after a crisis meeting in Morocco.

Following the meeting in Rabat, attended by Mr Infantino, secretary general Mattias Grafström and members of FIFA's management board, FIFA said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for the president while acknowledging that the handling of the withdrawn FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal should have been different.

In a statement, FIFA said a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologising for the errors and promising a review.

It added that, with the proposal withdrawn, FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process" and would take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Vehicles believed to be carrying Mr Infantino and Mr Grafström were seen leaving FIFA's Africa office in Sale after the meeting, which came amid mounting criticism of Mr Infantino's leadership ahead of next year's presidential election.

The meeting followed last week's withdrawal of a proposal to sell a 20 per cent stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion for football development.

The proposal, which also drew scrutiny because of the involvement of a company with family links to US President Donald Trump, prompted fierce criticism from European soccer's governing body UEFA and other stakeholders, who accused FIFA of poor governance and a lack of consultation.

Gianni Infantino's closeness to US President Donald Trump has been criticised. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

The apology underscored FIFA's acknowledgement that mistakes had been made in the handling of his proposal for a new commercial rights body, which has become the most serious challenge to his leadership since he became FIFA president in 2016 after triggering a torrent of criticism from UEFA, several member associations and senior FIFA officials over governance and consultation.

His backdown last Friday has done little to assuage those critics, most notably UEFA, which accused him of selling the soul of the game and has said it no longer has confidence in his leadership.

That has cast a shadow over Mr Infantino's re-election for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco in March, which had looked like a foregone conclusion two months ago.

A handful of European federations have withdrawn their backing for the Swiss Italian, but perhaps more damaging are the messages coming from Infantino's FIFA colleagues.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also questioned Mr Infantino's leadership on Wednesday, saying he has lost confidence in the FIFA president after learning senior advisers had not been consulted on the abandoned proposal.

"I don't have confidence in Mr Infantino," Mr Carney told reporters, adding that failing to inform senior executives and fellow board members of such a significant proposal "should be fatal" for any leader.

Mr Grafström had sent an internal memo to staff lamenting the "sad and reproachable series of events" that led to the project being "permanently abandoned", two sources told Reuters.

"Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue," the Swede added in the letter, which made no mention of Mr Infantino by name.

His words echoed those of FIFA's Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour, who said last week that staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned in protest at the plan last week. Arsene Wenger, FIFA's chief of Global Football Development, said he had not been involved in drafting the proposal, and called the decision to withdraw it "absolutely necessary".

Former Portugal great Luis Figo, who had planned to run for the FIFA presidency in 2015, said Infantino should resign over the affair, while UEFA Vice-President Laura McAllister told Reuters the controversy surrounding the abandoned proposal had brought the FIFA president's leadership to a crisis point.

Mr Infantino has spent the past week in Morocco, which will co-host the World Cup in 2030 and whose football association has announced its continued support for him.

Gianni Infantino has garnered the support of FIFA's executive, but many national governing bodies are sharpening their knives. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The meeting was widely seen as an effort to reinforce support for Mr Infantino and ensure that he emerges from the crisis with enough backing to remain the favourite for re-election in March.

An Extraordinary Congress could be called if 43 or more FIFA member associations make a formal written request for one.

Qatar, which hosted the 2022 World Cup, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Indonesia and the Philippines have declared their loyalty to Mr Infantino.

Mr Infantino has always enjoyed a lot of support away from the traditional heartlands of the game, where impoverished football associations rely on FIFA's largesse to operate.

But European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect clubs, players and fans.

It also criticised the "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition.

Leading African football administrators have sent messages of support as Mr Infantino looks to the continent's 54 members for backing. The African confederation (CAF) has yet to take a stance.

The executive committee of the smallest and least wealthy regional confederation, Oceania, will meet next Wednesday to discuss their approach.

Under FIFA rules, the vote of San Marino, whose men's team are ranked 211th and last in the world rankings, counts as much as that of World Cup winners like Brazil, Germany, Argentina and Spain.

One clear advantage for Mr Infantino as he looks to extend his presidency until 2031 is that no clear candidate to stand against him in March's election has yet emerged.

Jordan FA President Prince Ali bin Hussein has twice stood for the post, and he made his position clear on Tuesday when he accused FIFA of "blackmail", saying it had offered to help solve problems in exchange for endorsing Mr Infantino.

"We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now," Prince Ali wrote on social media.

A FIFA spokesperson rejected reports that Mr Infantino had made promises over the host of the 2030 World Cup final.

"It is false and misleading to claim the FIFA president has made any promise in relation to hosting the FIFA World Cup 2030 Final. A decision will be made by FIFA in due course," the spokesperson said.

title: Foragers concerned as ID apps misidentify toxic mushrooms
text:
Searching through the forest for wild mushrooms is an ancient and romantic tradition.

As the weather cools, foragers like Robbie Robinson head to the woods to hunt for gold.

The professional forager has spent more than 40 years gathering wild mushrooms and selling them to restaurants across Sydney and regional New South Wales.

Robbie Robinson has more than 40 years experience of foraging wild mushrooms. (ABC Central West: Emily Middleton)

"They're wild, so the nutrients that go into anything commercial or industrial are a very different set of nutrients compared to what's out here in the wild," Mr Robinson said.

"You get seasonal variation every year."

Wild mushrooms often grow in the undergrowth of pine plantations and state forests.

Popular edible mushrooms include the saffron milk cap and slippery jack, but identifying which mushrooms are safe to eat is a life-saving skill.

Some toxic varieties mimic safe varieties, with the most notorious being the death cap mushroom, which can cause severe illness and even death.

While it is legal to forage in NSW forests, NSW Health does not recommend it. (ABC Central West: Emily Middleton)

This poses a risk to amateur foragers and has led to the development of a range of digital tools to help identify safe varieties.

However, there are concerns these tools are leading foragers astray.

A recent study published in the scientific journal NPJ Science of Food found that AI-mediated mushroom identification tools tend to be inaccurate.

The researchers found the top-performing app failed to correctly identify the mushroom in nearly 15 per cent of cases.

The other tools were even less reliable, with one app providing incorrect information in over 90 per cent of tests.

Diego Bonetto has been teaching foraging for more than two decades. (Supplied: Helene Algie)

Find a guide

For more than 25 years, Lithgow-based expert forager and educator Diego Bonetto has said it is great to see more people picking wild produce.

But he is concerned about a noticeable increase in people using mobile phones to help them forage.

"You go out and harvest what you know is edible, and it's not going around trying to match the picture from the phone with what you're looking at in the fields," Mr Bonetto said.

" So go out with someone, at least for the first and second time, to know what to do. "

The wild mushroom season runs through late autumn and early winter. (Supplied: Diego Bonetto)

Mr Bonetto said amateur foragers should seek hands-on experience with mushrooms alongside an experienced picker.

"Mushroom foraging, like anything else, needs to be done in knowledge," he said.

" However, something new is the people with the assumption of knowledge. "

Life-threatening risk

While it is legal to forage in New South Wales state forests, the state's health department does not recommend picking and eating any wild mushrooms.

According to the Food Safety Information Council, the Australian Poisons Information Centre receives about 900 calls a year about people eating wild mushrooms, with about one in three cases requiring hospital treatment.

Consuming certain mushrooms can also be fatal, as shown by the high-profile Victorian case where three people died after consuming a beef wellington containing death cap mushrooms.

"If we think about mushrooms specifically, it's the fact that they are in some cases toxic, and in some cases are extremely toxic," UNSW associate professor of food microbiology Julian Cox said.

"In a food safety sense, anything could be contaminated within the natural environment by, say, faecal matter from various animals, and that might carry bad bugs from bacteria through to parasites."

Julian Cox says there is a potential risk of food safety issues in restaurant using foraged ingredients. (Supplied: UNSW)

Mr Cox said the "hand-me-down" process increases the risk of consuming a toxic mushroom.

"I always worry that one misstep, one bad pick, and that chef could be potentially causing harm to their patrons … but as adults, we pay our money and make our choice and take our chance.

"Going to a restaurant that is based on local produce, foraged ingredients, especially, I think it's important to say to people there is a potential risk of food safety issues."

Diego Bonetto, who was born in Italy, says mushroom foraging is an annual cultural tradition there. (Supplied: Aimee Crouch)

Wild mushrooms on the menu

While there are risks, there is a strong preference for wild mushrooms in chefs' kitchens.

Mr Robinson said much of the knowledge and education about foraging is passed down through word of mouth among chefs.

"I knew European chefs that had been using different wild mushrooms in Europe, and from that point of view they were very helpful in passing along knowledge to me," he said.

Robbie Robinson says some chefs prefer wild mushrooms over store-bought fungi. (Supplied: Helene Algie)

"I read a lot as well, I tracked down people who were already known for their foraging, so it was a combination of conversation, reading, and, of course, the most important thing is that you come out into the forest."

With the risk of a potential mix-up, Mr Robinson said it is ideal to forage at first with someone who knows what you can or cannot pick.

Once you have honed the skill, he said it is knowledge you do not lose.

"Once you've defined them by colour and smell and touch, it's like knowing that a rose is a rose and a daffodil is a daffodil, and you don't forget that knowledge and you take it with you for the rest of your life."

title: Can live performance recreate a crude horror story? Unfortunately, yes
text:
Advertisement

DANCE

CreepyPasta ★★

Dancehouse, Carlton

Until August 8 Creepypastas, for those who don’t know, are short but crude horror stories posted on the internet. And they really are awful. The prose is awkward, the pacing erratic and the content banal. Of course, that’s part of their grubby folkish charm: these are disposable, authorless texts, copied and pasted from forum to forum. Large LED screens loom large in Creepypasta. Darren Gill Can live performance create a creepypasta analogue? Unfortunately, yes. Harrison Hall and his new-media accomplices have pretty much nailed it. Its opening scene is the most effective. Three large LED screens face away from us, their dark backs looming over performer and co-choreographer Nikki Tarling. She, too, faces away, attached by a rope to one screen. Is she umbilically tethered to the machine?

Advertisement

It is a potent image, especially with the red status lights on the backs of the screens staring like little eyes. But once the screens are wheeled around, video content gradually takes over the performance. The live elements – dance and clowning – feel underdeveloped. Some of the material is comic, such as a video using Google Maps to explore the streets around the venue. And some of the material is more challenging, such as the lurid collages of digital detritus, which are accelerated and convulsive, and hard to watch for any length of time. Harrison Hall’s antics resemble creepypasta cosplay more than an embodied critique of technological alienation. Darren Gill Hall, meanwhile, naked except for a long, lank white wig, capers madly about the stage, and into the audience. He has plenty of energy, but there’s not much choreography. His antics resemble creepypasta cosplay more than an embodied critique of technological alienation. Perhaps all this is as it should be: a work modelled on creepypasta should be misshapen, excessive and slightly embarrassing. CreepyPasta captures the internet’s ugliness; as dance theatre, however, it is superfluous because we never see that ugliness landing in the body.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

MUSIC

Laufey | A Matter of Time Tour ★★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, until August 1 Ever dated someone and found them so boring, you wondered what you were doing there? That’s what Laufey asked us halfway through her first night back in Melbourne. The Icelandic-Chinese artist sits on the stairs built onto her stage, casually chatting to the crowd before launching into Bored . Laufey performs at Rod Laver Arena, July 30, 2026. Richard Clifford Laufey, 27, has cracked the code for making jazz a staple for her generation. She found fame online – from original work like debut single Street by Street, to jazz standard covers Misty and It’s Been a Long, Long Time. Then came three nights in the Palais Theatre in 2024, before a massive upgrade to Rod Laver Arena in 2026. The bright, whimsical Lover Girl comes early in Act I (across the show, silent movie-style projections divide the show into acts). Laufey twirls, claps and bounces in a blue dress straight from a fairytale book, and later moves across a castle-like stage structure for Dreamer – half damsel in distress, half determined girl-boss.

Advertisement

This act extends beyond the stage. Like any pop fandom, the uniform is clear – here, it’s coquette. Bows, earthy colours or pastels, then flowy skirts, or yellow or blue felt crowns. “I should’ve brought my bunny costume,” says one fan before the show, referring to Mei Mei the Bunny, the main character of the musician’s children’s book. Like any star with an ever-giving pop fandom, Laufey descends to high-five the crowd in Bored, and returns with a fan-made Australian flag with her face on it. “Revolution chic!” she reacts, one of her many witty one-liners of the night. “Hamilton could never.” 27-year-old Laufey has cracked the code for making jazz a staple for her generation. Richard Clifford She crowns a best-dressed fan, and shouts out two fans dressed as coffee and pie, a nod to Let You Break My Heart Again. Seriously, it doesn’t get any more jazz-pop than this. Act II brings us back to Laufey’s roots. A cover of Old Devil Moon, then jazz remixes of Haunted, Valentine, and Fragile. Her aura shifts from a twirling lover girl to an alluring vocalist as the stage becomes her jazz bar. The circus-like third act brings us Carousel, and the Swan Lake-esque Forget-Me-Not – an ode to her home, Iceland.

Advertisement

After an outfit change in Act IV, Laufey emerges in a showman-like set for an abundance of sass in Mr Eclectic, Madwoman and Tough Luck. This one’s a real emotional rollercoaster – she returns to the piano for Promise, the ultimate tear-jerker of the night. As always, Laufey continues to flex a widely ranged classical upbringing. She plays a guitar in Falling Behind, a piano in Too Little, Too Late, and plays the cello alongside twin and creative director Junia on the violin for Madwoman. Laufey twirls, claps, and bounces in a blue dress straight from a fairytale book Richard Clifford Before closing the act with From the Start, Laufey gets vulnerable about her struggle with beauty standards in Snow White. Perhaps the key to making jazz and bossa nova mainstream among Laufey’s generation, myself included, all boils down to relatability. A first crush, being “too much”, the most boring or character-altering relationship in your 20s, and struggling with body image – these are some core experiences she sings about. And perhaps we sing along to sing the feelings out. It’s therapeutic, vulnerable and heartfelt especially in a crowd of thousands. The night ends on a dark, ear-piercing note: Sabotage. The track that jump-scared the internet upon release. Whatever I heard when I flinched on my first listen, it was louder and more intense tonight. Three words sit on my notes app here: “WHAT THE HELL”.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews The success of a one-woman show lives and dies by its lead. This performer rises to the challenge The encore is surprisingly intimate for a pop show. The stage and orchestra rest for the night, and it’s just Laufey, her guitar, and us. She says bye (for now) with Letter To My 13-Year-Old Self, and fulfils a fan’s request to sing Slow Down. Laufey’s songs are intimate and warm; they feel right for a quiet day at home or a cafe on a rainy day. But her tour shows that her quiet can be loud, that intimacy can be scaled up – and that you sure as hell can belt out bossa nova and jazz – and maybe think about an ex or a crush – for four entire acts.

title: Helen Goh’s toasty and interesting new take on banana cake
text:
Malted banana loaf cake with toasted walnuts and (optional) espresso glaze. William Meppem

This loaf came about from wanting something in the spirit of banana bread but with a little more definition. Ripe bananas bring a delicious sweetness, but they can sometimes tip a cake towards one-note comfort, so I’ve added coffee and toasted walnuts to pull in the opposite direction: the coffee sharpening and deepening the flavour, and the walnuts adding gentle bitterness and texture. Alongside browned butter and malt, the result is darker, toastier and, I think, more interesting than a classic banana loaf.

Despite the relatively long ingredient list, the batter comes together in a single large saucepan, making it surprisingly easy to prepare.

The coffee icing is optional, but adds a little luxury and gives the final scattering of toasted walnuts something to cling to.

August 6, 2026 — 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We’re well past the midway point of the year, a time when the weight of being in the wrong job can feel the heaviest. At the start of this year, I gave some simple advice to anyone who was thinking about switching jobs. Many people return from the Christmas break with a new year resolution to change up their role – but it is the worst time to quit, because this is when the difference between the number of jobs advertised and number of people seeking jobs is greatest. August is the perfect time to quit your job, but many workers are too scared to. Tamara Voninski My advice in January was to wait until the mid-year, when this imbalance is reversed. Now we’re here, I bear good news for those itching to land a better job: August is, statistically speaking, the best month to look for work. According to data from Jobs and Skills Australia, there are strong levels of job advertisements but typically fewer applicants per role. As we approach the end of the year, this ratio reverses, so applying for a job now increases your chances from a strict mathematical point of view.

Advertisement

This year, however, we need to add a caveat, a pretty big one. The proportion of workers who are handing in their notice and deciding to move jobs over the past year has fallen to its lowest yet recorded. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows that our “job mobility rate” is now just 7.2 per cent of the workforce, meaning that about 1 million people changed jobs in the past 12 months. When you break it down by age, this trend is primarily led by younger workers who are switching jobs markedly less than in previous decades. When was the last time that you learnt something genuinely new at work? In common with many employees who have waited a long time to find secure work, they are cautious about making any sudden moves in a world that feels increasingly fragile. And for anyone who follows the global daily news, who can blame them? However, just because this might be theoretically the best time to switch jobs, deciding when it’s time to search for one is a decision only you can make. Consider your finances, your mental health, the market, your industry, your engagement levels and how much you’re getting from your current role.

Advertisement

I advise job hunters to apply a simple rule of thumb: to ask themselves when they last learnt something genuinely new at work. If, in the previous six to 12 months, the answer is nothing, then it might be time to think about a new role. Editor's pick Opinion

Jobs You’re probably ignoring this part of your CV. It could cost you Tim Duggan Work columnist This doesn’t always have to be in another company. Sometimes one meaningful conversation with your manager is all it takes to add new skills to your role, or to shift into another that might just be the change that you were looking for. Waiting too long in a stagnant role can easily backfire, as disengagement can turn into resentment the longer you stand still in a job that’s going nowhere. You are the only person in charge of your career, so take control of its direction before someone else forces you to. Many people have that niggling or nagging thought about whether it’s time to hand in the notice. If you’ve been waiting for a little nudge in the right direction, here it is.

LIV Golf has announced it has agreed terms with a “major investor” but failed to guarantee whether Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm will stay beyond this season. Scott O’Neil, the LIV chief executive, who took over from Greg Norman last year, confirmed on Wednesday (Thursday morning, AEST) that the golf league has signed a lifeline deal to continue beyond this season after the withdrawal of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF). There has been no announcement on the future of LIV Golf star Bryson DeChambeau. AP O’Neil claimed the unnamed investor was big enough to underwrite LIV for at least “2027, 28, 29 and 30” without the need for any other investors coming on board. In an earlier statement, LIV said the deal had already been approved by its board of directors, adding that it expected terms to be finalised “in the coming weeks, with the goal of entering a transaction in September”.

Advertisement

Speculation will nevertheless be rampant regarding the future of Rahm and DeChambeau, LIV’s two biggest names. Neither man has committed to the league following PIF’s decision to walk away at the end of this season after sinking US$5 billion ($7.1 billion) into the venture. During the press conference, O’Neil declined several times to confirm that DeChambeau or Rahm would remain part of the league, assuming it survives. Jon Rahm lines up a putt during LIV Golf’s event in Adelaide in February. Getty Images Asked directly whether the deal would allow LIV “to keep and afford stars, the likes of Bryson and Jon Rahm, going forward”, O’Neil gave a long and rambling answer about Major League Baseball and how the model had needed to change to attract younger fans. Asked a second time specifically about the importance of keeping DeChambeau and Rahm, O’Neil replied vaguely that LIV was “blessed with stars”, adding there was not “any bigger star on the planet in South Africa than Dean Burmester”.

Advertisement

O’Neil eventually said he would love DeChambeau and Rahm to “come along for the ride” but insisted that he had “enough support from enough players” for LIV to thrive regardless. “I think when you have a global game, and you have 57 players from 21 countries and you’re playing in 10 countries on five continents, how you define ‘stars’ gets really interesting,” O’Neil said. Australian Lucas Herbert is showered with champagne after his LIV Golf win in England last month. AP “So while I have all the time in the world for Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, I think I’d be remiss in saying they’re not only two of the biggest, best golfers on the planet, but I think they’re some of the biggest stars in sports, let alone golf. “We would certainly love them to come along for the ride and journey because they carry maybe more weight than anybody in the game and I have a lot of time for that.

Advertisement

“I think we have enough support from enough players, and we have such an interesting format and global format, I think we’ll do quite well in getting the right stars for this game.” O’Neil said he informed LIV’s players on Tuesday, after which DeChambeau led a players-only session. Jon Rahm and former LIV Golf boss Greg Norman in 2023. AP O’Neil was expected to tee it up in the LIV Golf New York Pro-Am later on Wednesday in a group with Australian Cameron Smith. Other groups in Wednesday’s Pro-Am include Eric Trump, the son of the US president, who is playing with Rahm. Donald Trump is not playing, although he is expected to attend this week. Trump won the senior and super-senior men’s club championships at the same course last weekend, later posting on Truth Social: “It’s called talent. I have it and they don’t.”

PIF announced on April 30 that it would pull the plug on LIV at the end of the season after investing more than $5bn in the venture. Related Video Video icon 1:04 Aussie dominates LIV Golf UK At that stage, LIV’s future looked shaky. Some of its highest-profile players – including Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed – walked away, and O’Neil was reportedly looking for investment ranging from $250m to $350m. Nor was there any guarantee of any profit for the next few years. A reimagined version of the league aimed to operate a 10-event annual schedule and projected profitability after three years. LIV Golf hired investment bank Ducera Partners to run the process. LIV Golf cancelled its New Orleans event in June, and it is unclear whether its season-ending team championship, which was scheduled to be held in Michigan later this month, will take place. O’Neil said LIV had “not made any final formal decisions” but “hope to in the coming weeks”.

If Michigan does not take place, the 2026 season will end with the Indianapolis event from August 20-23. O’Neil did say the league’s next phase would be “driven by and for the players”, who would be “majority equity holders” in LIV. He added there was no shame in being well paid. “The best people in the world at what they do should make a good living, and I don’t think there’s any shame in that,” he said. “So many of them came [to LIV] because this was a good opportunity for them to make some money, and this second bite at the apple is equity instead of cash. title: Money, money, money: Trump rakes in the cash from his social media posts
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsTrump's White House Opinion Money, money, money: Trump rakes in the cash from his social media posts Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 6, 2026 — 12:05pm

August 6, 2026 — 12:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The high-frequency traders who signed up to pay $US100,000 ($140,000) a month for early access to Donald Trump’s social media posts may already have had a demonstration of how easily they can more than recover their investments. On Saturday, Trump Media & Technology Group’s “Truth API” went live, giving subscribers to the service access to his posts on Truth Social milliseconds before his non-paying followers saw them. For the love of money: US President Donald Trump has found a way to further profit from his presidency. AP Hours after the API (application programming interface) creating a connection between the subscribers’ and Truth Social’s software was activated, Trump – who had been threatening Iran with massive air and missile strikes again, “the biggest attack since World War II” – posted that he had called off the attacks because America’s allies in the Middle East had reached the basic parameters of a deal to end the war, including a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The oil price, not surprisingly, fell heavily. It had traded above $US90 a barrel leading into the weekend. It fell below $US84 a barrel when futures trading closed on Friday, and dropped further on Monday.

Advertisement

There’s no doubt, Trump’s posts do move markets. Trump Media began sounding out Wall Street institutions about selling priority access to his posts last month, offering it at $US100,000 a month for a 12-month subscription and $US60,000 a month if they signed up for three years. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street Trump’s company is failing. This is his shady plan to give it a lifeline Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At least five Wall Street firms and several financial media businesses have already subscribed, the president’s company says. That, and a competitive advantage in trading – for high-frequency algorithmic traders, milliseconds are their business models and competitive advantage – will pressure other high-frequency traders to join. For a business that lost more than $US400 million in the first quarter on paltry revenue of just $US871,000, those subscriptions alone may already have more than double the $US3.7 million of revenue Trump Media generated last year.

Advertisement

Investors certainly think the new service will be material for the struggling company, with Trump Media’s shares jumping more than 16 per cent since markets became aware of the existence of the API plan. The service monetises for commercial gains – and personal gain for Trump, who owns 41 per cent of Trump Media – presidential announcements that are routinely made first in his Truth Social posts before any official White House announcement. ‘This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the president’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders.’ Democrat senators Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff Its unveiling has generated controversy and criticism, with Democrat senators Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff writing to the Securities and Exchange Commission demanding an investigation and suggesting that the service could violate insider trading laws. “This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the president’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders,” they wrote.

Advertisement

Trump Media responded by saying that its critics were lashing out against the Truth API “either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and non-public information.” Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s three-pronged threat to American democracy Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Effectively, Trump Media is arguing that Trump’s posts, and those of the other nine top posters on its platform made available via the API, are made available to all Truth Social subscribers at the same time – it’s just that those with access to the API can take advantage of a latency gap to get them fractions of a second earlier than those who don’t. There are other social media platforms that also have APIs, although they don’t have the President of the United States making official announcements on them. Truth API is just another way in which Trump is monetising a presidency that has already generated billions of dollars for him and his family.

Advertisement

In this instance, however, he is making money from something that doesn’t belong to him. Under the Presidential Records Act the US, not the president, has “complete ownership, possession and control” of any documents created or received by the president. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America ‘Trump Airport’ could be a new cash cow for the president’s empire Trump, of course, does have the immunity granted by the US Supreme Court for almost anything he does while in the White House and, in any case, it is up to the Republican-dominated Congress to police the legislation, and the party has shown no appetite or inclination to do anything that might upset Trump. Those who have subscribed to the API and trade based on its feed might be more vulnerable to charges of insider trading, assuming the SEC, led by Trump appointees, were willing to act.

Advertisement

That is, however, where Trump media’s argument comes into play that the Trump posts, along with those from vice-president JD Vance and Trump’s sons, aren’t made available to subscribers ahead of other users of the platform. It might look like institutionalised insider trading, but there are plenty of other situations, including at most major stock exchanges, where there are APIs or co-locations for high-frequency traders that enable them to gain an advantage over other market participants. Loading Those institutions that have signed up to the service know that $US1.2 million a year is only a fraction of what they might make from their early access to Trump’s market-sensitive posts, which tend to be voluminous and erratic and therefore have the potential to move financial markets regularly and materially. Trump’s posts on the state of play in the war in the Middle East in particular have routinely caused major movements, in either direction, in the pricing of oil futures. There are millions to be made from the latency gap.

Advertisement

There’s also an incentive for Trump to make even more pronouncements on Truth Social that are price-sensitive, given that it would enhance Trump Media’s revenues while validating the cost of the service for its subscribers. The pertinent question about the ethics of commercialising the president’s posts is whether, if he weren’t president, anyone would pay $US1.2 million a year for early access. Related Article Updated

Trump's White House Trump’s teleprompter aide allegedly made $US100,000 betting on his speeches The answer might have been provided by Trump Media itself. The discounted $US60,000-a-month pricing of three-year packages presumably reflects the fact that the Trump presidency now has only just over 16 months to run, in the normal course of events. The posts of Trump the ordinary citizen would have little, if any, value. Senate Democrats have introduced some legislation – the “Stop Corrupt Trading Act” and the “NO PROFIT ACT” in attempts to prevent a president, vice president and their families from selling real-time or non-public access, including prioritised real-time data feeds, to government statements.

Advertisement

At this point, those bills are unlikely to gain any traction in Congress. After the midterm elections, of course, that could change. For now, however, Trump has found a way to generate yet another income stream from this highly lucrative second stint in the White House. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. title: When to see a GP, visit urgent care or go to the emergency department this winter
text:
In Brief The Australian government has outlined three broad categories of care, each with varying symptom severity.

Chronic heart conditions, lung conditions, metabolic conditions, diabetes and kidney problems can all contribute to a worsening illness.

Getting the help you need for a winter illness could be simpler than spending hours waiting to be seen in a busy hospital emergency room.

That's the message the government is sending this flu season, a time when experts say hospitals tend to be the busiest, and wait times blow out.

While managing cold and flu cases is a national health concern, one state is taking a particularly strong stance, urging people to avoid the emergency room unless their lives are at risk.

On Monday, just under 10,000 people presented to emergency departments in Sydney, which the NSW health minister has described as the "biggest ever recorded winter day in history".

Professor Paul Griffin from the University of Queensland School of Medicine told SBS News that while numbers will vary between states, this time of year is often busy nationwide.

Across Australia, Griffin said healthcare services were seeing presentations of flu and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), as well as an increase in COVID-19 cases.

While these can be concerning conditions, an emergency room will always prioritise the most severe health conditions first, Griffin explained.

"If you don't need to go to your emergency department, it does free up valuable resources for them to be able to deal with more emerging cases," he said.

"There are a number of viable options for people that have conditions that are a little bit less urgent, and that's why we want people to make sure that they understand where the best place for them to go really is."

Where should you go?

It can depend on your symptoms and any underlying health conditions.

The Australian government has outlined three broad categories of care — routine, urgent and emergency — each with varying symptom severity, encompassing flu symptoms as well as broader conditions.

Most health issues can be addressed through routine care, which for many people means their GP.

Griffin said GPs are not only a good touchpoint for receiving care when sick but can also help you prepare a plan ahead of potential illness.

They can provide health checks, vaccinations and offer family and individual health advice.

"If it's something that you're not feeling needs urgent attention, then your GP is often the best place to start to get the care that you need," Griffin said.

Source: SBS News

If you start experiencing symptoms like chest pain or feel like a respiratory illness is worsening, you may want to consider going to an urgent care clinic (UCC) or the hospital.

"If you're breathing okay, even drinking okay, not systemically unwell, your GP is a really good place to start. If any of those things aren't the case, then I'd have a very low threshold for presenting to hospital," Griffin said.

"Whereas those urgent care clinics are really good for handling things that aren't imminently life-threatening and unlikely to require an admission to hospital."

Since 2023, the government has launched 137 urgent care clinics across the country.

"Medicare UCCs help reduce pressure on our hospitals and emergency departments, allowing them to focus on higher urgency and life-threatening conditions," a spokesperson for the Department of Health told SBS News.

Considerations for vulnerable Australians

Groups of people who are at highest risk for severe disease with respiratory viruses are Australians at the extremes of age: young children and older adults.

Griffin said that people who also have other medical conditions can be at further risk of illness.

"If you have a number of medical problems and you're an older adult and you get one of these respiratory viruses, it can certainly fairly rapidly progress to severe disease," he said.

Chronic heart conditions, lung conditions, metabolic conditions, diabetes and kidney problems can all contribute to a worsening illness.

"So understanding that risk, being proactive in having seen your GP or specialist before and having a plan is a really good way of managing the winter," Griffin said.

If you're not sure what kind of care is best for you, Griffin advised contacting a service such as Queensland's 13 HEALTH hotline or an after-hours GP for advice on the best escalation plan at the time.

The Australian government — through its free 1800MEDICARE service — also provides 24/7 health advice from registered nurses and connection to the right care, such as your regular GP, the local hospital or a Medicare UCC.

"In the after-hours period, and if clinically appropriate, callers may be offered a phone or video consultation with a 1800MEDICARE GP," the health department spokesperson said.

Not too late to act

Griffin said planning ahead with your GP is a great way to prepare for the winter flu season, as navigating complicated health services when you're sick can feel like an insurmountable task.

It's also not too late to vaccinate against common viruses.

"That includes influenza, and everyone should have one of those every year," Griffin said.

"For COVID, if you're high risk, it's probably every six to 12 months. But most people should get a COVID-19 vaccine once a year.

"And now with RSV vaccines being available, I'd certainly encourage anyone over 50 with medical problems or everyone over 70 to have had an RSV vaccine."

title: Kmart’s $89 glasses can record what you see. But what happens next?
text:
IN BRIEF AI smart glasses can record videos, make calls and translate speech or text in real time.

But experts have cautioned that the technology can be misused for dangerous or prohibited activity.

Kmart recently launched a new accessory — dubbed Camera Glasses — which it said blends stylish eyewear with built-in camera technology.

At a glance, the black-framed spectacles from Kmart's in-house brand Anko look like any ordinary pair of glasses. But by Monday 3 August, there were reports the product was sold out online.

At $89, the glasses provide a low-cost alternative to the smart glasses designed by glasses company Ray-Ban and Facebook owners Meta, which start at $337. The latest generation of this technology costs more than $700.

A recent promotional video for Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, featuring celebrity Kylie Jenner, showcased its features. Those include an ultra-HD camera, discreet open-ear Bluetooth speakers, and translation technology.

In July, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said people who don't wear smart glasses in the future will be at a "pretty significant cognitive disadvantage".
